analysis.one_liner: Bans agreements between employers not to hire each other's workers.
analysis.headline: The bill was never acted on: introduced in July 2023, referred to the Senate HELP Committee, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025 without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful for two or more employers—including through franchise or contractor agreements—to agree not to solicit or hire each other's current or former employees, or to threaten to enforce such an agreement. Workers harmed by such agreements could sue for actual damages plus punitive damages and attorney's fees, and the Federal Trade Commission would also enforce the ban. It would give workers a legal tool against employer 'no-poach' arrangements that limit their ability to switch jobs or get a raise.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, especially in industries where no-poach clauses are common, such as franchised food service and retail. These agreements limit outside hiring offers, which research on the economics of labor markets links to lower wages and reduced job mobility for employees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers in industries with no-poach deals

how_it_helps.text: It makes agreements between employers not to hire or solicit each other's employees unlawful, including when embedded in franchise or contractor-subcontractor agreements [S2].

It gives individual workers a right to sue for actual damages plus punitive damages, with attorney's fees and court costs awarded to a successful plaintiff, enforceable in any federal district court [S2].
It authorizes the Federal Trade Commission to enforce the ban with the powers it uses under the FTC Act, alongside the private right of action [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers and franchise companies that currently use or benefit from no-poach agreements: they would lose a tool that limits competition for their workers, face FTC enforcement, and become liable in private lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: Enforcing the ban through litigation could raise hiring and compliance costs for businesses, including small franchisees operating under franchise agreements, since the bill treats franchise agreements as a covered channel for restrictive employment agreements [S2].
As a single-section bill, it covers all employers regardless of size and provides no phase-in, so businesses would need to revise franchise and contractor documents immediately upon enactment [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward: workers keep the ability to receive outside job offers, which is one of the main routes to a raise. The costs fall on employers that would have to remove these clauses, and courts would have to define how far the ban reaches into ordinary franchise and contractor agreements. The bill is narrow and does not affect non-compete agreements between an employer and its own worker, only agreements between employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the End Employer Collusion Act on July 26, 2023, with Senator Elizabeth Warren [S1].
The same day it was introduced, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S4].
No further action was taken, and the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and franchise companies that rely on agreements not to hire each other's workers are better off, because they keep that tool and avoid the new liability and FTC enforcement the bill would have created. Workers remain without a federal private right of action against these agreements.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on July 26, 2023

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were ever taken on the bill; it had one Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor, so its broader partisan shape was never tested.

industries.industry: Franchised food service and retail chains
industries.note: These companies have commonly included no-poach provisions in franchise agreements, which limit other franchisees from hiring each other's workers; the bill would make such agreements unlawful and create liability for workers who sue [S2].

The bill covers contractor-subcontractor agreements, so staffing intermediaries could no longer enforce terms restricting poaching of workers, but firms that do not use such clauses would face little change [S2].
